questions.q: A student heats a white solid in a sealed glass tube and wants to find out whether the heating changed the composition of the solid. Which measurement, made before and after heating, would answer the question?
options: The total mass of the sealed tube and its contents
The color of the solid under the same lighting
The physical state of the solid at room temperature
The percent by mass of each element in the solid
optionWhy: A student who thinks mass changes in a chemical reaction picks this. Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, so the total mass of the sealed tube stays the same whether the change is physical or chemical.

A student who thinks a color change always shows a chemical change picks this. A change in color is possible evidence only; the color of a solid can change, for example with particle size, without any change in composition.

A student who thinks a change of phase produces a new substance picks this. A substance can change phase without any change in composition, so the state of the sample does not show whether its composition changed.

Composition is the proportion of each element in a substance. If the percent by mass of an element differs after heating, the solid is a new substance and a chemical change occurred; if it is the same, the composition did not change.
questions.explain: Composition is the proportion of each element in a substance. If the percent by mass of an element differs after heating, the solid is a new substance and a chemical change occurred; if it is the same, the composition did not change.
questions.working: Composition is the proportion of each element in a substance, so the needed quantity is the percent by mass of each element in the solid before and after heating. The total mass of a sealed tube does not change in either a physical or a chemical change, and color or phase can change without a change in composition.

questions.q: The diagram at the top represents a small sample of liquid water. When the water boils, bubbles form in the liquid. Which numbered diagram best represents the particles inside one of the bubbles?
optionWhy: A student who thinks boiling breaks water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen picks this. Boiling separates whole H₂O molecules from one another; the bonds within each molecule are not broken, so no H₂ or O₂ forms.

A student who thinks particles expand when they are heated picks this. The molecules in the vapor are the same size as in the liquid; the gas takes up more space because the molecules are much farther apart.
Boiling is a physical change: water molecules escape from the liquid and are far apart in the vapor, but each is still an H₂O molecule of the same size. The bubble is water vapor.

A student who thinks the bubbles in boiling water are air picks this. Bubbles form throughout the boiling liquid as water turns to vapor, and they carry the water away, so they contain H₂O molecules, not nitrogen and oxygen.
questions.explain: Boiling is a physical change: water molecules escape from the liquid and are far apart in the vapor, but each is still an H₂O molecule of the same size. The bubble is water vapor.
questions.working: Boiling is a change of phase, a physical change: H₂O molecules leave the liquid intact and are far apart in the vapor; they do not split into H₂ and O₂, do not grow larger, and are not replaced by air.

questions.q: A student uses the apparatus shown to boil a solution of sodium chloride, NaCl, in water until about half of the liquid has boiled away. Which prediction about the liquid that collects in the receiving flask is correct?
options: It is water with no NaCl in it, and it boils at the same temperature as pure water
No liquid collects, because boiling decomposes the water into hydrogen and oxygen
It is a solution of NaCl, because the dissolved NaCl evaporates along with the water
It is a new liquid compound that boils at a different temperature from water
optionWhy: Boiling and condensing are physical changes. Water vaporizes, travels through the condenser, and condenses as liquid water in the receiving flask; NaCl does not vaporize at this temperature and stays in the boiling flask. The collected liquid is water and has the properties of water.

A student who thinks boiling breaks water molecules apart picks this. The vapor is H₂O, which condenses back to liquid water in the condenser; decomposing water into H₂ and O₂ is a chemical change that boiling does not cause.

A student who thinks a dissolved solid leaves with the water vapor picks this. NaCl does not vaporize at the boiling point of water, so it stays behind in the boiling flask and the condensed liquid contains no NaCl.

A student who thinks a change of phase produces a new substance picks this. Water vapor and liquid water are both H₂O; condensing the vapor gives back water with the same composition and boiling point.
questions.explain: Boiling and condensing are physical changes. Water vaporizes, travels through the condenser, and condenses as liquid water in the receiving flask; NaCl does not vaporize at this temperature and stays in the boiling flask. The collected liquid is water and has the properties of water.

questions.q: Which numbered diagram best represents the solute particles in an aqueous solution of sodium sulfate, Na₂SO₄? Water molecules are not shown.
optionWhy: A student who thinks soluble ionic compounds dissolve as intact formula units picks this. In solution the Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions separate from one another and move independently among the water molecules.
A student who thinks the subscripts stay attached to the ions picks this, showing Na₂²⁺ particles. The subscript 2 in Na₂SO₄ means two separate Na⁺ ions per formula unit; there is no Na₂²⁺ ion.

A student who thinks polyatomic ions break apart when an ionic compound dissolves picks this. The S and O atoms of SO₄²⁻ are held together by covalent bonds, and the sulfate ion stays intact in solution.

Na₂SO₄ is a soluble ionic compound, so in water it separates into its ions: each formula unit gives two Na⁺ ions and one SO₄²⁻ ion. The sulfate ion is a polyatomic ion and stays intact. Two formula units give four Na⁺ and two SO₄²⁻ ions moving independently.
questions.explain: Na₂SO₄ is a soluble ionic compound, so in water it separates into its ions: each formula unit gives two Na⁺ ions and one SO₄²⁻ ion. The sulfate ion is a polyatomic ion and stays intact. Two formula units give four Na⁺ and two SO₄²⁻ ions moving independently.

questions.q: Solid calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂, dissolves in water. Which of the following equations correctly represents this physical process?
optionWhy: A student who thinks the subscripts stay with the ions writes the two nitrate ions as one (NO₃)₂²⁻ particle. The subscript 2 means two separate NO₃⁻ ions, written 2 NO₃⁻(aq).

Dissolving separates the ionic compound into its ions without changing them: one Ca²⁺ ion and two intact NO₃⁻ ions per formula unit. Atoms and charge balance, and no new substance forms, so the equation describes a physical process.

A student who thinks a dissolved ionic compound is present as neutral atoms or molecules of its elements writes Ca, N₂, and O₂. Dissolving separates the compound into the ions it already contains, Ca²⁺ and NO₃⁻; each nitrate ion stays intact and no elements are formed.

A student who thinks an ion's subscript in a formula equals its own charge reads the 2 after the nitrate group as a 2− charge on one nitrate ion. The subscript counts ions: there are two NO₃⁻ ions, each with a 1− charge, and this equation does not conserve N or O atoms.
questions.explain: Dissolving separates the ionic compound into its ions without changing them: one Ca²⁺ ion and two intact NO₃⁻ ions per formula unit. Atoms and charge balance, and no new substance forms, so the equation describes a physical process.
questions.working: Ca(NO₃)₂ is a soluble ionic compound: each formula unit separates into one Ca²⁺ ion and two NO₃⁻ ions, and each nitrate ion stays intact. Ca(NO₃)₂(s) → Ca²⁺(aq) + 2 NO₃⁻(aq). Check: Ca 1, N 2, O 6 on each side; charge 0 = (2+) + 2(1−).

questions.q: When aqueous solutions of lead(II) nitrate, Pb(NO₃)₂, and potassium iodide, KI, are mixed, a yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide, PbI₂, forms. Which of the following is the balanced net ionic equation for the reaction?
optionWhy: A student who thinks (aq) means anything in the water writes the precipitate as aqueous. PbI₂ forms as an undissolved solid, so it is written PbI₂(s).

A student who thinks the spectator ions react to form the soluble product writes K⁺ and NO₃⁻ combining. Potassium nitrate stays dissolved as separate K⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions, which are unchanged; the ions that change are Pb²⁺ and I⁻, which form solid PbI₂.

K⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions, so the net ionic equation shows only the ions that form the precipitate: one Pb²⁺ and two I⁻ give PbI₂(s). Atoms balance (1 Pb, 2 I) and charge balances (0 on each side).

A student who thinks dissolved ionic compounds are present as neutral atoms or molecules of their elements writes Pb and I₂. In solution lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide provide Pb²⁺ and I⁻ ions, which are what combine.
questions.explain: K⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions, so the net ionic equation shows only the ions that form the precipitate: one Pb²⁺ and two I⁻ give PbI₂(s). Atoms balance (1 Pb, 2 I) and charge balances (0 on each side).
questions.working: Molecular: Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2 KI(aq) → PbI₂(s) + 2 KNO₃(aq). Complete ionic: Pb²⁺(aq) + 2 NO₃⁻(aq) + 2 K⁺(aq) + 2 I⁻(aq) → PbI₂(s) + 2 K⁺(aq) + 2 NO₃⁻(aq). Removing the spectators K⁺ and NO₃⁻: Pb²⁺(aq) + 2 I⁻(aq) → PbI₂(s). Check: Pb 1 = 1, I 2 = 2; charge (2+) + 2(1−) = 0 = 0.

questions.q: The top diagram represents a mixture of SO₂(g) and O₂(g) in a sealed container. The gases react according to the equation 2 SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 SO₃(g). Which numbered diagram best represents the contents of the container after the reaction has gone to completion?
optionWhy: A student who reads the coefficients as the actual number of particles that react picks this diagram: 2 SO₂ and 1 O₂ have formed 2 SO₃, and the other 2 SO₂ and 1 O₂ are left unreacted. Coefficients give a ratio, so the remaining SO₂ and O₂, which are in the same 2 : 1 ratio, react as well.

A student who multiplies the coefficient into the formula picks this diagram, in which the product is drawn as S₂O₆ particles. The atoms are conserved, but 2 SO₃ means two separate SO₃ molecules, each with one S atom, not one particle that contains two S atoms.

The coefficients give the ratio 2 SO₂ : 1 O₂ : 2 SO₃. The box holds 4 SO₂ and 2 O₂, exactly this ratio, so the reaction uses all of both reactants and forms 4 separate SO₃ molecules. The 4 S atoms and 12 O atoms present before the reaction are all present afterward.

A student who thinks the number of molecules is conserved picks this diagram, which has 6 molecules after the reaction as there were 6 before. Atoms are conserved, not molecules: 6 SO₃ would need 6 S atoms and 18 O atoms, but only 4 S atoms and 12 O atoms are present.
questions.explain: The coefficients give the ratio 2 SO₂ : 1 O₂ : 2 SO₃. The box holds 4 SO₂ and 2 O₂, exactly this ratio, so the reaction uses all of both reactants and forms 4 separate SO₃ molecules. The 4 S atoms and 12 O atoms present before the reaction are all present afterward.

questions.q: The particle diagrams represent the substances present in a sealed container before and after a reaction in the gas phase. Which equation is the best symbolic representation of the reaction shown?
optionWhy: A student who multiplies a coefficient into the formula picks this, writing the two CO₂ molecules as C₂O₄ and the two H₂O molecules as H₄O₂. The atom totals are right, but the diagram shows the products as separate CO₂ and H₂O molecules, which are written 2 CO₂ and 2 H₂O.

The diagram shows one C₂H₄ molecule and three O₂ molecules before the reaction, and two separate CO₂ molecules and two separate H₂O molecules after it. Each formula matches a particle in the diagram and each coefficient is the number of those particles; there are 2 C, 4 H and 6 O atoms on each side.
A student who writes a diatomic element as separate atoms picks this. The diagram shows the six O atoms joined in pairs, as three O₂ molecules; 6 O would mean six separate O atoms.

A student who treats an equation as a tally of the atoms of each element in each substance picks this: 6 O atoms before, and C₂O₄ and H₄O₂ for the atoms in the carbon-containing and hydrogen-containing products. An equation must also show how the atoms are grouped into particles: 3 O₂, 2 CO₂ and 2 H₂O.
questions.explain: The diagram shows one C₂H₄ molecule and three O₂ molecules before the reaction, and two separate CO₂ molecules and two separate H₂O molecules after it. Each formula matches a particle in the diagram and each coefficient is the number of those particles; there are 2 C, 4 H and 6 O atoms on each side.

questions.q: A student is drawing a particulate representation of the reaction represented by the equation 2 Al(s) + 3 Cl₂(g) → 2 AlCl₃(s). The student's 'before' box contains 6 Cl₂ molecules. How many Al atoms should the 'before' box contain, and how many AlCl₃ formula units should the 'after' box contain, if no reactant is to be left over?
optionWhy: A student who reads the coefficients as the actual numbers of particles picks this, copying the 2 in front of Al and of AlCl₃. Two Al atoms react with only 3 Cl₂ molecules, so 3 of the 6 Cl₂ molecules would be left over.

A student who thinks reactant particles combine one-to-one picks this, matching each Cl₂ molecule with one Al atom. The ratio is 2 Al to 3 Cl₂, and 6 AlCl₃ units would need 18 Cl atoms when only 12 are present.
A student who applies the ratio of coefficients upside down picks this: 6 × 3/2 = 9. The ratio is 2 Al for every 3 Cl₂, so 6 Cl₂ molecules require 6 × 2/3 = 4 Al atoms.

The coefficients give the ratio 2 Al : 3 Cl₂ : 2 AlCl₃. Six Cl₂ molecules is twice the 3 Cl₂ of the equation, so twice the 2 Al and twice the 2 AlCl₃ are needed: 4 Al atoms and 4 AlCl₃ units. Check: 12 Cl atoms before, 4 × 3 = 12 Cl atoms after.
questions.explain: The coefficients give the ratio 2 Al : 3 Cl₂ : 2 AlCl₃. Six Cl₂ molecules is twice the 3 Cl₂ of the equation, so twice the 2 Al and twice the 2 AlCl₃ are needed: 4 Al atoms and 4 AlCl₃ units. Check: 12 Cl atoms before, 4 × 3 = 12 Cl atoms after.
questions.working: Ratio from the coefficients: 2 Al : 3 Cl₂ : 2 AlCl₃. Al atoms = 6 Cl₂ × (2 Al / 3 Cl₂) = 4. AlCl₃ units = 6 Cl₂ × (2 AlCl₃ / 3 Cl₂) = 4. Atom check: 4 Al and 12 Cl before; 4 AlCl₃ contain 4 Al and 12 Cl. Distractors: coefficients copied, 2; one-to-one, 6; ratio inverted, 6 × 3/2 = 9.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the changes in bonds and attractions that occur as solid sodium chloride, NaCl(s), dissolves in water?
options: Ionic bonds between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ break, and ion-dipole attractions to water form
Attractions between NaCl molecules break, and the molecules spread out among water molecules
Covalent bonds in water molecules break, and new NaOH and HCl molecules then form
All bonds in NaCl break, and separate Na and Cl atoms spread out among water molecules
optionWhy: Solid NaCl consists of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by ionic bonds. As it dissolves, these ionic bonds are broken and the separated ions are attracted to the polar water molecules: Na⁺ to the O ends and Cl⁻ to the H ends.

A student who thinks ionic compounds are made of molecules picks this. Solid NaCl contains no NaCl molecules; it is a lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, and these ions separate from one another as it dissolves.

A student who thinks dissolving a salt is a reaction with water that forms new compounds picks this. The water molecules stay intact; the ions separate from the lattice and are surrounded by water molecules, and evaporation recovers NaCl.

A student who thinks a dissolving substance breaks up into separate atoms picks this. The particles in solution are Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, the same charged particles that make up the solid, not neutral atoms.
questions.explain: Solid NaCl consists of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by ionic bonds. As it dissolves, these ionic bonds are broken and the separated ions are attracted to the polar water molecules: Na⁺ to the O ends and Cl⁻ to the H ends.
questions.working: No calculation. NaCl(s) is a lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. On dissolving, the ionic bonds between the ions are broken and each ion becomes surrounded by water molecules held by ion-dipole interactions; the water molecules stay intact.

questions.q: Which of the following processes involves the breaking of covalent bonds?
options: Melting a sample of ice at 0°C
optionWhy: A student who thinks hydrogen bonds are the O–H bonds inside a water molecule picks this. Melting overcomes some hydrogen bonds between separate water molecules; the covalent O–H bonds within each molecule stay intact.
A student who thinks boiling breaks the covalent bonds within molecules picks this. Boiling separates whole ethanol molecules from one another; the vapor still consists of ethanol molecules.
A student who thinks a dissolving substance breaks up into its atoms picks this. Sugar dissolves as intact molecules surrounded by water molecules; no covalent bonds within the sugar molecules break.

In 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂ the atoms are rearranged into new substances: O–O and O–H bonds in H₂O₂ are broken and new bonds form in H₂O and O₂. This is a chemical process; the other three involve only changes in intermolecular interactions.
questions.explain: In 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂ the atoms are rearranged into new substances: O–O and O–H bonds in H₂O₂ are broken and new bonds form in H₂O and O₂. This is a chemical process; the other three involve only changes in intermolecular interactions.
questions.working: No calculation. Melting ice and boiling ethanol are phase changes: only intermolecular attractions change. Dissolving sugar separates intact sugar molecules. Decomposing hydrogen peroxide, 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂, breaks O–O and O–H bonds and forms new O–H and O=O bonds.

questions.q: A sealed flask contains a small amount of liquid bromine, Br₂. The flask is warmed until all of the bromine has vaporized. The diagrams show the flask's contents before warming and four possible representations of the contents afterward. Which numbered diagram best represents the contents of the flask after warming?
optionWhy: A student who thinks boiling breaks the covalent bonds within molecules picks this. Vaporizing bromine only separates Br₂ molecules from one another; the Br–Br bonds stay intact, so the vapor consists of Br₂ molecules, not Br atoms.

Vaporization overcomes the intermolecular attractions between Br₂ molecules but does not break the Br–Br bonds. The flask is sealed, so the same six molecules are present; they keep their size and spread out to fill the container.
A student who thinks a substance loses particles or mass when it becomes a gas picks this. The flask is sealed, so all six Br₂ molecules remain inside; the gas has the same mass as the liquid did.

A student who thinks particles expand when heated picks this. The Br₂ molecules keep their size; the gas occupies more of the flask because the molecules are farther apart, not because they are larger.
questions.explain: Vaporization overcomes the intermolecular attractions between Br₂ molecules but does not break the Br–Br bonds. The flask is sealed, so the same six molecules are present; they keep their size and spread out to fill the container.
questions.working: No calculation. Vaporization is a physical process: only intermolecular attractions are overcome. The six Br₂ molecules stay intact, keep their size and stay in the sealed flask, but spread out to fill it. The diagram with six same-sized Br₂ molecules spread through the box is correct.

questions.q: The diagram labeled Before reaction represents a mixture of N₂ and H₂ molecules in a sealed container. The gases react according to the equation N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g). Which numbered diagram best represents the contents of the container after the reaction has gone to completion?
optionWhy: Each N₂ molecule reacts with three H₂ molecules, so the 6 H₂ molecules react with 2 N₂ molecules: H₂ is limiting. They form 4 NH₃ molecules, and 1 N₂ molecule is left over. All 6 N atoms and 12 H atoms are accounted for.

A student who thinks every reactant is used up when a reaction goes to completion picks this. Only 2 of the 3 N₂ molecules are needed for the 6 H₂ molecules, so one N₂ molecule must remain; this diagram has lost two N atoms.

A student who takes the reactant present in fewer molecules, N₂, as the limiting reactant picks this, converting all 3 N₂ into 6 NH₃. That would need 9 H₂ molecules, but only 6 are present, and the diagram shows 18 H atoms where there were 12.

A student who reads the coefficient in 2 NH₃ as forming one N₂H₆ molecule picks this. The coefficient 2 means two separate NH₃ molecules, so the product should be drawn as NH₃ molecules, each with one N atom and three H atoms.
questions.explain: Each N₂ molecule reacts with three H₂ molecules, so the 6 H₂ molecules react with 2 N₂ molecules: H₂ is limiting. They form 4 NH₃ molecules, and 1 N₂ molecule is left over. All 6 N atoms and 12 H atoms are accounted for.

questions.q: A mixture of 3.00 g of H₂(g) and 16.0 g of O₂(g) reacts according to the equation 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(l). What is the maximum mass of H₂O that can form?
optionWhy: A student who thinks every reactant is used up completely picks this, adding 3.00 g and 16.0 g. Only 2.0 g of the H₂ reacts; about 1.0 g remains, so the water formed has a mass of 18.0 g.

n(O₂) = 16.0/32.00 = 0.500 mol and n(H₂) = 3.00/2.016 = 1.49 mol. O₂ needs twice its moles of H₂, 1.00 mol, which is available, so O₂ is limiting. It forms 2 × 0.500 = 1.00 mol H₂O, or 18.0 g; about 1.0 g of H₂ is left over.

A student who takes the reactant with the smaller mass, H₂, as limiting picks this: 1.49 mol H₂ → 1.49 mol H₂O = 26.8 g. In moles there is more H₂ (1.49 mol) than the 1.00 mol the O₂ can use, so O₂ is limiting.

A student who thinks the mass of a product equals the mass of the reactant it came from picks this, taking the 16.0 g of O₂ that reacts as the mass of water. The water also contains the 2.0 g of H₂ that reacts: 1.00 mol H₂O is 18.0 g.
questions.explain: n(O₂) = 16.0/32.00 = 0.500 mol and n(H₂) = 3.00/2.016 = 1.49 mol. O₂ needs twice its moles of H₂, 1.00 mol, which is available, so O₂ is limiting. It forms 2 × 0.500 = 1.00 mol H₂O, or 18.0 g; about 1.0 g of H₂ is left over.
questions.working: n(H₂) = 3.00 g ÷ 2.016 g/mol = 1.49 mol; n(O₂) = 16.0 g ÷ 32.00 g/mol = 0.500 mol. 0.500 mol O₂ needs 1.00 mol H₂, and 1.49 mol is present, so O₂ is limiting. n(H₂O) = 2 × 0.500 = 1.00 mol; mass = 1.00 mol × 18.02 g/mol = 18.0 g. (H₂ left over: 0.49 mol, 0.98 g.)

questions.q: A 10.00 mL sample of H₂SO₄(aq) of unknown concentration is titrated with 0.2000 M NaOH(aq) to a phenolphthalein endpoint. The reaction is H₂SO₄(aq) + 2 NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2 H₂O(l). The initial buret reading is 10.20 mL and the final buret reading is 25.20 mL. What is the molarity of the H₂SO₄(aq)?
optionWhy: A student who thinks the moles of titrant and analyte are equal at the equivalence point picks this, taking 3.000 × 10⁻³ mol H₂SO₄. The balanced equation shows that each H₂SO₄ reacts with two NaOH, so only 1.500 × 10⁻³ mol H₂SO₄ was present.
The NaOH delivered is 25.20 − 10.20 = 15.00 mL, or 3.000 × 10⁻³ mol. The equation needs 2 mol NaOH per mole of H₂SO₄, so n(H₂SO₄) = 1.500 × 10⁻³ mol in 0.01000 L: 0.1500 M.
A student who takes the final buret reading as the volume delivered picks this, using 25.20 mL. The buret started at 10.20 mL, so only 15.00 mL of NaOH was delivered.

A student who thinks the analyte and titrant have equal concentrations at the equivalence point picks this. The equivalence point is defined by moles in the stoichiometric ratio; the H₂SO₄ concentration must be calculated from the moles of NaOH used.
questions.explain: The NaOH delivered is 25.20 − 10.20 = 15.00 mL, or 3.000 × 10⁻³ mol. The equation needs 2 mol NaOH per mole of H₂SO₄, so n(H₂SO₄) = 1.500 × 10⁻³ mol in 0.01000 L: 0.1500 M.

questions.q: A sample of HCl(aq) is titrated with NaOH(aq), using phenolphthalein as the indicator. Which numbered diagram best represents the solute particles in a small volume of the solution in the flask at the equivalence point? Water molecules are not shown.
optionWhy: At the equivalence point the HCl has been totally consumed by the OH⁻ added, forming water, with no OH⁻ left over. The solute particles left are Na⁺ from the titrant and Cl⁻ from the analyte, equal in number and separate from each other.

A student who thinks equal amounts of acid and base remain together at the equivalence point picks this. H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ react with each other to form water, so they cannot both remain in amounts comparable to the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
A student who thinks a dissolved ionic product exists as molecules picks this. NaCl is ionic: in solution the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are separate, each surrounded by water molecules.

A student who treats the endpoint color, which needs a slight excess of base, as defining the equivalence point picks this. The diagram shows OH⁻ and extra Na⁺ from titrant added beyond the equivalence point; at the equivalence point the moles of OH⁻ added equal the moles of HCl, so none is left over.
questions.explain: At the equivalence point the HCl has been totally consumed by the OH⁻ added, forming water, with no OH⁻ left over. The solute particles left are Na⁺ from the titrant and Cl⁻ from the analyte, equal in number and separate from each other.

questions.q: Aqueous solutions of AgNO₃ and KI are mixed in a beaker, and a yellow solid settles. The diagram represents the ions in the beaker after mixing; water molecules are not shown. Which statement about the reaction is supported by the diagram?
options: The Ag⁺ and I⁻ ions have come together, keeping their charges, to form the solid
The Ag⁺ ions have gained electrons from the I⁻ ions to form the solid
The K⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions have bonded together to form dissolved KNO₃ units
The K⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions have been used up along with the others in the solid
optionWhy: The solid at the bottom of the beaker is drawn as Ag⁺ and I⁻ ions packed together, each still carrying its charge. This is a precipitation reaction: ions combine to form an insoluble ionic compound, AgI(s), with no transfer of electrons.
A student who thinks ions must become neutral atoms to form a solid picks this. The diagram shows the particles in the solid still labeled Ag⁺ and I⁻, so no electrons have been transferred.
A student who thinks the leftover ions join into formula units of the soluble product picks this. The diagram shows the K⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions far apart: they remain separate, unchanged ions in solution.
A student who thinks all the ions are used up when a precipitate forms picks this. The diagram shows three K⁺ and three NO₃⁻ ions still in the solution; only Ag⁺ and I⁻ are in the solid.
questions.explain: The solid at the bottom of the beaker is drawn as Ag⁺ and I⁻ ions packed together, each still carrying its charge. This is a precipitation reaction: ions combine to form an insoluble ionic compound, AgI(s), with no transfer of electrons.

questions.q: Which of the following is the balanced equation for the complete combustion of propane, C₃H₈(g)?
optionWhy: A student who thinks oxygen combines only with the carbon, with the hydrogen released as H₂, picks this. In complete combustion the hydrogen also combines with oxygen, forming H₂O.

A student who sets the coefficient of O₂ equal to the number of O atoms in the products (10) picks this. Each O₂ supplies two O atoms, so 5 O₂ are needed; this equation has 20 O atoms on the left and 10 on the right.

A student who thinks burning leaves the carbon behind as a solid picks this. The atoms balance, but solid carbon forms only when combustion is incomplete; in complete combustion the carbon ends up as CO₂.
The products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon are CO₂ and H₂O. Three C atoms give 3 CO₂ and eight H atoms give 4 H₂O; these contain 10 O atoms, supplied by 5 O₂.
questions.explain: The products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon are CO₂ and H₂O. Three C atoms give 3 CO₂ and eight H atoms give 4 H₂O; these contain 10 O atoms, supplied by 5 O₂.
questions.working: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon: reactants are the hydrocarbon and O₂; products are CO₂ and H₂O. C: 3 → 3 CO₂. H: 8 → 4 H₂O. O atoms in products: 3(2) + 4(1) = 10, supplied by 5 O₂. C₃H₈(g) + 5 O₂(g) → 3 CO₂(g) + 4 H₂O(g).

questions.q: A solution of the weak acid HA is titrated with NaOH(aq). The diagram represents the solute particles in a small volume of the solution in the flask at one point during the titration; Na⁺ ions and water molecules are not shown. At which point in the titration was the solution represented?
options: Before any NaOH has been added
optionWhy: A student who thinks HA and A⁻ are equal at the equivalence point picks this. At the equivalence point almost all of the HA has been converted, so the diagram would show A⁻ ions and almost no HA.

Six acid units were present at the start; three have been converted to A⁻ by the added OH⁻ and three remain as HA. Half of the acid has been neutralized, which is the half-equivalence point, where [HA] = [A⁻].
A student who thinks a weak acid at equilibrium is about half ionized picks this. Before base is added, a weak acid solution is mostly HA with very little A⁻.
A student who thinks equal amounts of an acid and its conjugate base give a neutral solution picks this. With [HA] = [A⁻], pH = pK_a of HA, which for a typical weak acid is well below 7.
questions.explain: Six acid units were present at the start; three have been converted to A⁻ by the added OH⁻ and three remain as HA. Half of the acid has been neutralized, which is the half-equivalence point, where [HA] = [A⁻].
questions.working: No calculation. Equal numbers of HA and A⁻ (3 and 3): half of the HA originally present (6 units) has been converted to A⁻ by OH⁻. This is the half-equivalence point.

questions.q: The titration curve shown was obtained when a 20.0 mL sample of a weak acid was titrated with 0.10 M NaOH. How many acidic protons does each molecule of the acid have?
optionWhy: A student who counts only the large rise near 40 mL as an equivalence point picks this. The smaller rise at 20 mL is also an equivalence point.
A student who counts the flat regions, including the one after 40 mL, picks this. The flat region after the last equivalence point shows excess NaOH and corresponds to no proton.
The curve has two steep rises, at 20 mL and at 40 mL, equally spaced. Each equivalence point marks the removal of one proton, so each molecule has two acidic protons.
A student who counts every bend in the curve, including the middle of each flat region, picks this. Only the two steep rises are equivalence points.
questions.explain: The curve has two steep rises, at 20 mL and at 40 mL, equally spaced. Each equivalence point marks the removal of one proton, so each molecule has two acidic protons.
questions.working: Count the steep rises (equivalence points): one at 20 mL (about pH 3.7 to 5.8) and one at 40 mL (about pH 8 to 11). Two equivalence points, equally spaced: two acidic protons.
